Harness is competing for the decision about what ships to production, and its benchmark defines what it must show before an AI scan can block a merge. ## What Is Covered in This Article: * What Harness’s LLMScanBench Q3 2026 found about LLM security scanning, and two related Harness posts on pipeline scanning and decision models. * Why the decision about what ships to production is where Harness is competing. * Why a merge gate needs verdict stability, and what Harness has and hasn’t shown. * How GitHub, OpenAI, and Harness each treat AI security findings at the merge. * What Harness, its competitors, and platform and security leaders should do next. **The News:** On September 28, 2026, Harness published LLMScanBench Q3 2026. It ran GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, both through OpenAI Codex Security’s security skills and with no human in the loop, against Harness AI SAST, its static application security testing (SAST) tool, on three intentionally vulnerable Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) applications. Harness reports that the LLM scanners posted 85% to 100% precision but low recall, with GPT-5.5 ahead of Opus 4.8 in most cases, and took 1.6 to 37 times longer and cost 6 to 39 times more than AI SAST. Three Opus 4.8 runs on unchanged WebGoat code returned recall of 16.2%, 19.7%, and 35.5%. Harness concludes that LLM scanners are “a harder fit for scanning regular PRs or code commits today.” It recommends them for penetration testing and periodic deep scans, and in pipelines, using LLMs “to validate and reason on the results of traditional scanners and to identify novel vulnerabilities.” Two related posts show how Harness applies those findings. A September 23 post describes Harness Security Testing Orchestration (STO), which is built on OpenAI Codex Security and runs an LLM scan on every pull request; the post does not state its availability or pricing. An October 5 post describes an application security (AppSec) classifier that flags customer API endpoints that call an LLM. It is built on Jev, a TypeSafe AI decision model that returns a probability rather than text. Harness routes the cases Jev is least sure about to an LLM. Details are in [Harness’s LLMScanBench Q3 2026 benchmark post](https://www.harness.io/blog/llmscanbench-q3-2026-choosing-the-right-approach-for-ai-vulnerability-discovery). ## Harness Shows Why LLM Security Scanning Needs a Repeatable Verdict **Analyst Take:** [Harness](https://www.harness.io/) lets customers configure an LLM security scan to stop a release. highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Tech firms launch custom AI chips for data centre inference Microsoft announced its Maia 300 custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip, designed for AI models across its data centres. The company plans large-scale deployments of its Azure Maia systems in 2027. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 14, 2026 at 09:00 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Microsoft announced Maia 300, its next-generation custom AI chip for data centre workloads. * Large-scale deployments of Azure Maia systems are planned for 2027, becoming the primary inference platform. * Google, Amazon, and OpenAI are also deploying custom chips to control AI inference costs and efficiency. * The shift aims to improve computing per dollar spent and manage power consumption in data centres. [Microsoft](/tag/microsoft) has announced Maia 300, its next-generation custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip, designed to run AI models across its data centres. The company plans to begin large-scale deployments of its Azure Maia systems in 2027. These chips are expected to become the primary inference platform for its products and services. Other major technology companies are also deploying custom chips for [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference). These include [Google](/tag/google) with its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and [Amazon](/tag/amazon) with its Trainium chips. [OpenAI](/tag/openai) also plans an inference chip, Jalapeño, with Broadcom. This shift is driven by the need to control inference costs, improve efficiency, and gain greater control over hardware supply and infrastructure planning. AI computing involves training models and then using them for inference tasks. Inference becomes a recurring operating expense as AI tools become more widely used. Every query or AI interaction consumes computing resources. Custom chips can be designed around a company's models, software, and expected workloads. This potentially improves computing delivered per rupee or dollar spent on hardware and electricity. Power consumption is another key consideration for data centres. Improving AI tokens generated per unit of energy can help companies serve more requests within existing power constraints. Custom silicon provides greater control over hardware supply and infrastructure planning. Companies may reduce external accelerator purchases and optimise system interaction. However, chip design involves significant development costs and manufacturing considerations. These factors affect the final budget. Microsoft's Maia 300 builds on earlier Maia processors. Maia 200 is already serving production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot. The Maia 300 architecture is designed for long-context reasoning and memory-intensive processing. Its planned uses include Copilot and GitHub Copilot. Microsoft's strategy coordinates chip design with its cloud infrastructure and AI software. This allows it to optimise the entire system for its services. Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Innovation, told Axios that Microsoft prioritises Maia for inference. She described it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing. Google has developed TPUs for years and uses them to support its AI models. In April 2026, Google announced its eighth-generation TPU systems, TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference. Amazon is pursuing a similar strategy with its Trainium family. The tests examined whether smaller models deployed locally could meet the demands of regulated business environments. Connect compared a baseline small language model, a domain-tuned version of the same model, and an orchestrated ensemble that assigned separate tasks to specialist models. Across the study, Connect evaluated 19 models in 52 professional domains using sequential editing workflows. Researchers found that, after 20 sequential interactions, frontier models lost or corrupted an average of 25% of document content during extended multi-turn exchanges. The benchmark used Connect AI Elly, the company's 4-billion-parameter model stack, to measure performance on representative enterprise datasets. The baseline setup, described as a single untuned compact model, scored 72.67% overall. Domain tuning lifted that score to 81.20%, with strong gains in insurance sentiment analysis and medical question answering. The orchestrated setup scored 85.42%, a 12.75 percentage-point improvement on the baseline and roughly 13 percentage points above the untuned single-model approach. The orchestrated configuration split workflows into separate functions, including domain routing, entity extraction, summarisation, retrieval and re-ranking, verification, and safety classification. The report argued that this division of labour improved evidence recall as well as financial and clinical summarisation. It also found that the orchestrated stack outperformed several named foundation models in cross-domain testing, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Amazon Nova, Mixtral-8x22B and Qwen3-14B. According to the findings, it also exceeded Claude in some healthcare and insurance tasks. The results highlight a growing debate in enterprise AI deployment, particularly in sectors that handle sensitive customer and patient information. Businesses in finance, healthcare and insurance are under pressure to improve automation and retrieval accuracy while maintaining tighter control over how data is processed and where it is stored. The issue is especially relevant in contact centres, where AI tools are increasingly used to summarise conversations, extract key details and retrieve policy or case information. Errors in those workflows can create operational and compliance problems if systems omit facts, misstate numbers or produce unsupported answers. Alfredo Gemma, AI Solution Director, Connect, said: "As organisations move beyond experimentation and start deploying AI into operational workflows, there is growing demand for models that are smaller, faster, more cost-effective, and easier to run in controlled environments. Workday logo visible on screen. Workday announced a wave of new AI agent capabilities and the acquisition of C1.ai at its annual Workday Rising event in Las Vegas this week. These advancements aim to automate routine tasks and enhance the user experience for Workday's HR, payroll, and finance applications, according to a recent report by CRN. The cloud application giant unveiled new AI agentic technologies, including autopilot agents, designed to perform various functions across its HR, payroll, and financial management applications. A key announcement was the agreement to acquire C1.ai, a developer of agentic identity technology. This acquisition is intended to bolster Workday's identity and access management capabilities, allowing for real-time governance of agents and their access to Workday and other enterprise systems. Workday also introduced its new front-end user experience, leveraging Sana, an AI agent technology acquired last year, which will serve as the central landing page for users. Additionally, new products like Work Intelligence and Workday Decision Intelligence were debuted, aiming to provide insights into job skills and enable real-time strategic decision-making for finance and HR managers. These developments signal a significant push into AI for Workday, with CEO Aneel Bhusri describing the event as a "re-founding moment" for the company. highlights.content: [Skip To Main Content](#primary-content) [News](/content/www/us/en/newsroom/home.html) # Announcing Intel® Inference Microservices: Tuned LLM Inference on Intel® Processors Intel® Inference Microservices make it easy to get tuned LLM performance on existing Intel® processors, eliminating days of complex, manual hardware optimization. Copied [Artificial Intelligence (AI)](/content/www/us/en/newsroom/home.html#aiartificialintelligence) ![](https://intelcorp.scene7.com/is/image/intelcorp/intel-inference-microservices?qlt=80&ts=1791990190915&dpr=off) Getting a large language model to respond is easy. Getting it to respond well, repeatedly, on the hardware you already own is the part that can take a week. Precision, how work is distributed across cores, how memory is laid out across NUMA nodes, and which instruction sets the engine uses all depend on both the model and the processor beneath it. Change the model and the good settings change. Move to a different generation of silicon and they change again. Intel® is announcing **Intel® Inference Microservices**. Each microservice is a container that serves one model behind an OpenAI compatible API and configures itself for the Intel® processor it detects at startup, using settings Intel® tuned and validated for that model on that silicon. You pick the model. The container picks the settings. This first release runs on Intel® Xeon® processors, and it is the first step toward a single inference interface across Intel® hardware. A microservice serves one model on one host. When you need a fleet of them, shared across teams with security and routing already handled, the [Intel® AI for Enterprise Inference](https://github.com/intel/enterprise-inference) toolkit provides that layer. # Try It Now The example below serves Qwen3-4B. You need a 4th, 5th, or 6th Gen Intel® Xeon® processor and Docker: ``` docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \   --cap-add SYS_NICE    --shm-size=2g \ ​​​​​​​  intel/inference-xeon-qwen-qwen3-4b:0.1.0 ``` That is the only command. On startup the container inspects the processor it landed on, selects the best available configuration profile for that model on that hardware, and applies it for you. There is nothing for you to tune and nothing to work out first. The first start takes a few minutes while the weights download. Wait for /health, then send it a request straight from the terminal: ``` curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \   -d '{     "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-4B",     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]   }' ``` That is the whole integration. No custom protocol, no Intel® SDK, no Python environment to build, and no engine to install. Most AI frameworks already speak the OpenAI API, so pointing one at that base URL is all it takes: the OpenAI SDK, LangChain, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, and Haystack all work unchanged, streaming included. **What It Changes for the Business** * Faster time to production, at the tuned configuration. Tuning, benchmarking, and adjusting for each model on each platform is replaced by a pull and a run, and what you pull is the configuration that performed best in Intel® Hardware. * No new hardware to procure. Inference becomes a scheduling decision against Intel® Xeon® capacity you already own, not a capital purchase, so a project can start this quarter rather than after a procurement cycle. * A wider pool of developers can ship AI. Application developers change a base URL. Deploying a model no longer needs an inference optimization specialist, which is the bottleneck most enterprise AI programs actually hit. * One pattern to standardize on. A validated profile plus a pinned tag means the same model behaves the same way on every matching host, under Docker and under Kubernetes alike. * What you build now carries forward. highlights.title: Sentient launches open benchmark to test AI model ownership
highlights.titleZh: Sentient launches open benchmark to test AI model ownership
highlights.content: [![Quartz](https://static.qz.com/quartz-v1.137.0/_next/static/media/quartz-logo.1poxn91047rb6.svg?dpl=1nln7blm5540)](/) [A.I.](/tech-innovation/ai) # Sentient launches first open benchmark to test AI model ownership Sentient’s open benchmark tests whether AI model fingerprints can withstand attacks and provide reliable evidence of model origin. [By Jake Cole](/author/jake_coe)·5 min read·Updated October 14, 2026 This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse. [Add QZ to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=qz.com) AI developers are exploring ways to establish where models originated, but research suggests that existing fingerprinting techniques may be easier to remove than their creators expect. As artificial intelligence models become easier to copy, modify, and redistribute, proving where they came from is becoming a more complicated problem. Model weights can circulate without their original documentation, while fine-tuning and distillation can produce systems that retain much of a model’s functionality without preserving an obvious record of its source. The [Sentient Foundation’s Fingerprinting Leaderboard](https://fingerprint.sentient.foundation/) aims to address that challenge by providing an open benchmark for comparing techniques designed to identify AI models. The platform is intended to evaluate how well fingerprints survive attempts to remove them and how much they affect model performance. The initiative follows research by Sentient-affiliated researchers and collaborators showing that fingerprinting techniques can remain vulnerable even when they perform well under conventional testing conditions. In the paper, [“Are Robust LLM Fingerprints Adversarially Robust?”](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2509.26598), researchers developed adaptive attacks against 10 proposed fingerprinting schemes, finding that all could be bypassed while maintaining high model utility. The findings highlight a broader challenge for AI developers: Embedding a fingerprint is one thing, but ensuring that it remains detectable when someone actively tries to remove it is another. AI model fingerprinting attempts to make a model identifiable through signals embedded in, or detectable from, its behavior. Rather than relying exclusively on metadata, ownership records or training logs, these methods seek evidence that can be tested against a suspected derivative model. Sentient’s approach embeds hidden behavioral signatures during training. A model owner can subsequently submit specially designed challenge prompts to a suspected derivative and analyze its responses for traces of the original fingerprint. The approach could provide an additional way to investigate whether a model originated from another developer’s work. Its effectiveness, however, depends on whether the identifying signals survive subsequent training and modification. “AI models are becoming some of the most valuable intellectual property in the world, yet once a model is copied or distilled, proving ownership becomes incredibly difficult,” said Sachi Kamiya, director of venture and growth at Sentient Foundation. “Fingerprinting puts the proof inside the model,” Kamiya said. “Think of it as the AI equivalent of the hidden marks Renaissance painters used to establish authorship.” The underlying issue extends beyond attribution. Developers releasing models for public use may want to encourage experimentation without losing the ability to demonstrate that their work has been reused. More reliable provenance techniques could help support that goal, although a fingerprint alone would not necessarily establish legal ownership or prove that copying was unauthorized. Research presented at NeurIPS 2025 demonstrated that fingerprinting can operate at considerable scale. highlights.content: [Sign In](https://bondoro.com/signin) [Bondoro](https://bondoro.com) [Sign In](https://bondoro.com/signin) Case Summary: Character.AI Chapter 11 19 min read Share [Case Summaries](/tag/case-summaries/) [Case Summaries](/tag/case-summaries/) # Case Summary: Character.AI Chapter 11 Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 amid child-safety litigation, multistate regulatory scrutiny and persistent cash burn, pursuing a 363 process anchored by Disney's $20 million stalking horse bid for a non-exclusive license to its AI technology after most of its workforce joined Disney. By [Insights](/author/insights/) ![Case Summary: Character.AI Chapter 11 Post image](/content/images/size/w2000/2026/10/characterai_feature-image.webp) > A deck version of this summary is also available [HERE](https://bondoro.com/content/files/2026/10/Character-Technologies_Deck-Summary_10.14.26.pdf). --- ### **Business Description** Character Technologies, Inc. d/b/a Character.AI ("Character" or the "Debtor"), operates Character.AI, an AI entertainment platform on which users interact with AI chatbot characters that are fictional or imagined. The platform, which began as one-on-one chat, now also generates images, video and audio alongside the conversation. Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas left Google and founded Character in 2021. The platform opened to the public as a beta in September 2022. In March 2023, Character closed a $150 million Series A round led by Andreessen Horowitz at a $1 billion valuation, with participation from earlier investors. Two months later, Character announced [c.ai+](https://blog.character.ai/introducing-c-ai/?ref=bondoro.com), an opt-in subscription plan, and released its first iOS and Android apps. The Debtor reports approximately 12 million monthly active users worldwide, who spend approximately 120 minutes a day on the platform on average. Revenue comes primarily from subscriptions and in-app advertising, with in-app purchases added in early 2026, and totaled approximately $23.6 million in fiscal year 2025. > [Character Technologies, Inc.](https://app.bondoro.com/preview/cases/Character_Technologies_Inc?ref=bondoro.com) filed for Chapter 11 protection on October 12, 2026 (the "Petition Date") in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, reporting $50 million to $100 million in both assets and liabilities. --- ### **Corporate History** ##### The 2024 Google Transaction In August 2024, Character entered into a transaction with Google (the “2024 Transaction”) in which Google paid approximately [$2.7 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204424000118/goog-20240930.htm?ref=bondoro.com) in cash for a non-exclusive license to Character’s large language model (“LLM”) technology and a release of certain claims Character may have had against Google and certain other parties, and rehired Character’s founders. The 2024 Transaction also served as a liquidity event for Character’s shareholders. Its venture investors were reportedly bought out at a valuation of approximately [$2.5 billion](https://www.axios.com/2024/08/05/google-characterai-venture-capital?ref=bondoro.com), and [EM360Tech](https://em360tech.com/tech-articles/character-ai-scraps-building-llms-after-google-deal?ref=bondoro.com), reporting on interim CEO Dominic Perella's interview with the Financial Times, said Character used the proceeds to fund that buyout, transfer ownership to employees through a co-operative structure and make a one-off payout to staff, while approximately 20% of its employees left for Google DeepMind. Consistent with those reports, all of Character’s equity holders as of the Petition Date are current or former directors or employees, and no corporation owns 10% or more of the Debtor. The 2024 Transaction also marked the end of Character’s effort to build its own models. Before the deal, Character trained its own LLM from scratch, according to [Andreessen Horowitz](https://a16z.com/2023/03/23/investing-in-character-ai/?ref=b...

The cloud application giant unveiled new AI agentic technologies, including autopilot agents, designed to perform various functions across its HR, payroll, and financial management applications. A key announcement was the agreement to acquire C1.ai, a developer of agentic identity technology. This acquisition is intended to bolster Workday's identity and access management capabilities, allowing for real-time governance of agents and their access to Workday and other enterprise systems. Workday also introduced its new front-end user experience, leveraging Sana, an AI agent technology acquired last year, which will serve as the central landing page for users. Additionally, new products like Work Intelligence and Workday Decision Intelligence were debuted, aiming to provide insights into job skills and enable real-time strategic decision-making for finance and HR managers. These developments signal a significant push into AI for Workday, with CEO Aneel Bhusri describing the event as a "re-founding moment" for the company. AI-generated illustration by The Tech Buzz. Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).· AI-generated image Database infrastructure just got a major shake-up. CedarDB is positioning its unified database engine as the answer to AI agents' insatiable appetite for real-time data processing, bridging the traditional divide between transactional and analytical workloads. As agentic AI systems proliferate across enterprises, the startup's timing couldn't be better - these AI agents need to read and write data simultaneously while making split-second decisions. The database world is witnessing a fundamental shift, and [CedarDB](https://cedardb.com) thinks it has the architecture to capitalize on it. The startup's unified database engine promises to handle both transactional processing and analytics in a single system - a technical feat that's becoming critical as AI agents reshape how enterprises interact with data. Traditionally, companies have been forced into an uncomfortable choice: optimize databases for either fast transactions (OLTP) or complex analytics (OLAP), but never both. This split has created expensive, complex infrastructure stacks where data constantly shuttles between systems. But AI agents don't have patience for that architectural baggage. "AI agents need to read historical patterns while simultaneously writing new transactions," explains the fundamental challenge driving CedarDB's approach. Unlike human users who can wait for batch processing or overnight data syncs, [AI agents demand real-time access to both operational and analytical data](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/ai-agents-promise-privacy-but-can-openai-and-meta-deliver) as they make autonomous decisions. Advertisement The timing aligns perfectly with the enterprise AI agent boom. Companies are rapidly deploying agentic AI systems that need to query customer histories, update inventory records, analyze market trends, and execute transactions - often within milliseconds of each other. The traditional approach of maintaining separate OLTP and OLAP systems creates latency bottlenecks that can cripple AI agent performance. CedarDB's unified architecture eliminates these data silos by redesigning the database engine from the ground up. The system can process high-volume transactions while simultaneously running complex analytical queries on the same data set, without the performance penalties that typically plague hybrid approaches. This isn't just a technical curiosity - it's becoming a business imperative. As [AI agents surge across industries](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/ai-agents-surge-drives-internet-infrastructure-stock-rally), enterprises are discovering that their existing database infrastructure wasn't built for the autonomous, data-hungry nature of agentic AI. These systems need to correlate vast amounts of historical data while updating records in real-time, a use case that breaks traditional database architectures. Advertisement The market opportunity is substantial. Enterprise database spending continues to grow...

By [Ivan Ferrari](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/expert/ivan-ferrari/) At this year’s [Jackson Hole symposium](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/jackson-hole-global-central-bankers-glimpse-dystopian-ai-future-2026-08-31/), Princeton economist Markus Brunnermeier warned central bankers that AI agents operating at scale could outmaneuver regulators and make markets more erratic. He argued that central bank transparency “arms the opponent,” which is to say the market, and particularly once artificial intelligence (AI) can predict policy. He suggested [two press conferences](https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-08-31/jackson-hole-global-central-bankers-glimpse-dystopian-ai-future): one for humans, and one for machines, designed as training data. The problem: AI can listen to both. Policymakers have been reckoning with how AI affects payments, tokenization, monetary policy, and financial stability ever since it morphed into acting. Back in August, a US appeals court [lifted](https://www.reuters.com/business/retail-consumer/amazon-loses-us-court-ban-perplexitys-ai-shopping-tools-2026-08-04/) an injunction that had barred Perplexity’s shopping agent from Amazon, ruling that when an agent acts on a user’s instruction, it is the user who accesses the platform. Amazon has since [blocked](https://www.geekwire.com/2026/amazon-blocks-metas-muse-ai-assistant-in-new-standoff-over-agentic-shopping/) Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, in a similar dispute over how autonomous software interacts with existing platforms. Elsewhere, the White House has [called](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/07/45470/) for autonomous laboratories and AI-run research. Harness is competing for the decision about what ships to production, and its benchmark defines what it must show before an AI scan can block a merge. ## What Is Covered in This Article: * What Harness’s LLMScanBench Q3 2026 found about LLM security scanning, and two related Harness posts on pipeline scanning and decision models. * Why the decision about what ships to production is where Harness is competing. * Why a merge gate needs verdict stability, and what Harness has and hasn’t shown. * How GitHub, OpenAI, and Harness each treat AI security findings at the merge. * What Harness, its competitors, and platform and security leaders should do next. **The News:** On September 28, 2026, Harness published LLMScanBench Q3 2026. It ran GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, both through OpenAI Codex Security’s security skills and with no human in the loop, against Harness AI SAST, its static application security testing (SAST) tool, on three intentionally vulnerable Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) applications. Harness reports that the LLM scanners posted 85% to 100% precision but low recall, with GPT-5.5 ahead of Opus 4.8 in most cases, and took 1.6 to 37 times longer and cost 6 to 39 times more than AI SAST. Three Opus 4.8 runs on unchanged WebGoat code returned recall of 16.2%, 19.7%, and 35.5%. Harness concludes that LLM scanners are “a harder fit for scanning regular PRs or code commits today.” It recommends them for penetration testing and periodic deep scans, and in pipelines, using LLMs “to validate and reason on the results of traditional scanners and to identify novel vulnerabilities.” Two related posts show how Harness applies those findings. A September 23 post describes Harness Security Testing Orchestration (STO), which is built on OpenAI Codex Security and runs an LLM scan on every pull request; the post does not state its availability or pricing. An October 5 post describes an application security (AppSec) classifier that flags customer API endpoints that call an LLM. It is built on Jev, a TypeSafe AI decision model that returns a probability rather than text. Harness routes the cases Jev is least sure about to an LLM. Details are in [Harness’s LLMScanBench Q3 2026 benchmark post](https://www.harness.io/blog/llmscanbench-q3-2026-choosing-the-right-approach-for-ai-vulnerability-discovery). ## Harness Shows Why LLM Security Scanning Needs a Repeatable Verdict **Analyst Take:** [Harness](https://www.harness.io/) lets customers configure an LLM security scan to stop a release. The tests examined whether smaller models deployed locally could meet the demands of regulated business environments. Connect compared a baseline small language model, a domain-tuned version of the same model, and an orchestrated ensemble that assigned separate tasks to specialist models. Across the study, Connect evaluated 19 models in 52 professional domains using sequential editing workflows. Researchers found that, after 20 sequential interactions, frontier models lost or corrupted an average of 25% of document content during extended multi-turn exchanges. The benchmark used Connect AI Elly, the company's 4-billion-parameter model stack, to measure performance on representative enterprise datasets. The baseline setup, described as a single untuned compact model, scored 72.67% overall. Domain tuning lifted that score to 81.20%, with strong gains in insurance sentiment analysis and medical question answering. The orchestrated setup scored 85.42%, a 12.75 percentage-point improvement on the baseline and roughly 13 percentage points above the untuned single-model approach. The orchestrated configuration split workflows into separate functions, including domain routing, entity extraction, summarisation, retrieval and re-ranking, verification, and safety classification. The report argued that this division of labour improved evidence recall as well as financial and clinical summarisation. It also found that the orchestrated stack outperformed several named foundation models in cross-domain testing, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Amazon Nova, Mixtral-8x22B and Qwen3-14B. According to the findings, it also exceeded Claude in some healthcare and insurance tasks. The results highlight a growing debate in enterprise AI deployment, particularly in sectors that handle sensitive customer and patient information. Businesses in finance, healthcare and insurance are under pressure to improve automation and retrieval accuracy while maintaining tighter control over how data is processed and where it is stored. The issue is especially relevant in contact centres, where AI tools are increasingly used to summarise conversations, extract key details and retrieve policy or case information. Errors in those workflows can create operational and compliance problems if systems omit facts, misstate numbers or produce unsupported answers. LLMs.content: [Skip To Main Content](#primary-content) [News](/content/www/us/en/newsroom/home.html) # Announcing Intel® Inference Microservices: Tuned LLM Inference on Intel® Processors Intel® Inference Microservices make it easy to get tuned LLM performance on existing Intel® processors, eliminating days of complex, manual hardware optimization. Copied [Artificial Intelligence (AI)](/content/www/us/en/newsroom/home.html#aiartificialintelligence) ![](https://intelcorp.scene7.com/is/image/intelcorp/intel-inference-microservices?qlt=80&ts=1791990190915&dpr=off) Getting a large language model to respond is easy. Getting it to respond well, repeatedly, on the hardware you already own is the part that can take a week. Precision, how work is distributed across cores, how memory is laid out across NUMA nodes, and which instruction sets the engine uses all depend on both the model and the processor beneath it. Change the model and the good settings change. Move to a different generation of silicon and they change again. Intel® is announcing **Intel® Inference Microservices**. Each microservice is a container that serves one model behind an OpenAI compatible API and configures itself for the Intel® processor it detects at startup, using settings Intel® tuned and validated for that model on that silicon. You pick the model. The container picks the settings. This first release runs on Intel® Xeon® processors, and it is the first step toward a single inference interface across Intel® hardware. A microservice serves one model on one host. When you need a fleet of them, shared across teams with security and routing already handled, the [Intel® AI for Enterprise Inference](https://github.com/intel/enterprise-inference) toolkit provides that layer. # Try It Now The example below serves Qwen3-4B. You need a 4th, 5th, or 6th Gen Intel® Xeon® processor and Docker: ``` docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \   --cap-add SYS_NICE    --shm-size=2g \ ​​​​​​​  intel/inference-xeon-qwen-qwen3-4b:0.1.0 ``` That is the only command. On startup the container inspects the processor it landed on, selects the best available configuration profile for that model on that hardware, and applies it for you. There is nothing for you to tune and nothing to work out first. The first start takes a few minutes while the weights download. Wait for /health, then send it a request straight from the terminal: ``` curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \   -d '{     "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-4B",     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]   }' ``` That is the whole integration. No custom protocol, no Intel® SDK, no Python environment to build, and no engine to install. Most AI frameworks already speak the OpenAI API, so pointing one at that base URL is all it takes: the OpenAI SDK, LangChain, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, and Haystack all work unchanged, streaming included. **What It Changes for the Business** * Faster time to production, at the tuned configuration. Tuning, benchmarking, and adjusting for each model on each platform is replaced by a pull and a run, and what you pull is the configuration that performed best in Intel® Hardware. * No new hardware to procure. Inference becomes a scheduling decision against Intel® Xeon® capacity you already own, not a capital purchase, so a project can start this quarter rather than after a procurement cycle. * A wider pool of developers can ship AI. Application developers change a base URL. Deploying a model no longer needs an inference optimization specialist, which is the bottleneck most enterprise AI programs actually hit. * One pattern to standardize on. A validated profile plus a pinned tag means the same model behaves the same way on every matching host, under Docker and under Kubernetes alike. * What you build now carries forward. LLMs.content: [![Quartz](https://static.qz.com/quartz-v1.137.0/_next/static/media/quartz-logo.1poxn91047rb6.svg?dpl=1nln7blm5540)](/) [A.I.](/tech-innovation/ai) # Sentient launches first open benchmark to test AI model ownership Sentient’s open benchmark tests whether AI model fingerprints can withstand attacks and provide reliable evidence of model origin. [By Jake Cole](/author/jake_coe)·5 min read·Updated October 14, 2026 This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse. [Add QZ to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=qz.com) AI developers are exploring ways to establish where models originated, but research suggests that existing fingerprinting techniques may be easier to remove than their creators expect. As artificial intelligence models become easier to copy, modify, and redistribute, proving where they came from is becoming a more complicated problem. Model weights can circulate without their original documentation, while fine-tuning and distillation can produce systems that retain much of a model’s functionality without preserving an obvious record of its source. The [Sentient Foundation’s Fingerprinting Leaderboard](https://fingerprint.sentient.foundation/) aims to address that challenge by providing an open benchmark for comparing techniques designed to identify AI models. The platform is intended to evaluate how well fingerprints survive attempts to remove them and how much they affect model performance. The initiative follows research by Sentient-affiliated researchers and collaborators showing that fingerprinting techniques can remain vulnerable even when they perform well under conventional testing conditions. In the paper, [“Are Robust LLM Fingerprints Adversarially Robust?”](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2509.26598), researchers developed adaptive attacks against 10 proposed fingerprinting schemes, finding that all could be bypassed while maintaining high model utility. The findings highlight a broader challenge for AI developers: Embedding a fingerprint is one thing, but ensuring that it remains detectable when someone actively tries to remove it is another. AI model fingerprinting attempts to make a model identifiable through signals embedded in, or detectable from, its behavior. Rather than relying exclusively on metadata, ownership records or training logs, these methods seek evidence that can be tested against a suspected derivative model. Sentient’s approach embeds hidden behavioral signatures during training. A model owner can subsequently submit specially designed challenge prompts to a suspected derivative and analyze its responses for traces of the original fingerprint. The approach could provide an additional way to investigate whether a model originated from another developer’s work. Its effectiveness, however, depends on whether the identifying signals survive subsequent training and modification. “AI models are becoming some of the most valuable intellectual property in the world, yet once a model is copied or distilled, proving ownership becomes incredibly difficult,” said Sachi Kamiya, director of venture and growth at Sentient Foundation. “Fingerprinting puts the proof inside the model,” Kamiya said. “Think of it as the AI equivalent of the hidden marks Renaissance painters used to establish authorship.” The underlying issue extends beyond attribution. Developers releasing models for public use may want to encourage experimentation without losing the ability to demonstrate that their work has been reused. More reliable provenance techniques could help support that goal, although a fingerprint alone would not necessarily establish legal ownership or prove that copying was unauthorized. Research presented at NeurIPS 2025 demonstrated that fingerprinting can operate at considerable scale. LLMs.content: [Sign In](https://bondoro.com/signin) [Bondoro](https://bondoro.com) [Sign In](https://bondoro.com/signin) Case Summary: Character.AI Chapter 11 19 min read Share [Case Summaries](/tag/case-summaries/) [Case Summaries](/tag/case-summaries/) # Case Summary: Character.AI Chapter 11 Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 amid child-safety litigation, multistate regulatory scrutiny and persistent cash burn, pursuing a 363 process anchored by Disney's $20 million stalking horse bid for a non-exclusive license to its AI technology after most of its workforce joined Disney. By [Insights](/author/insights/) ![Case Summary: Character.AI Chapter 11 Post image](/content/images/size/w2000/2026/10/characterai_feature-image.webp) > A deck version of this summary is also available [HERE](https://bondoro.com/content/files/2026/10/Character-Technologies_Deck-Summary_10.14.26.pdf). --- ### **Business Description** Character Technologies, Inc. d/b/a Character.AI ("Character" or the "Debtor"), operates Character.AI, an AI entertainment platform on which users interact with AI chatbot characters that are fictional or imagined. The platform, which began as one-on-one chat, now also generates images, video and audio alongside the conversation. Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas left Google and founded Character in 2021. The platform opened to the public as a beta in September 2022. In March 2023, Character closed a $150 million Series A round led by Andreessen Horowitz at a $1 billion valuation, with participation from earlier investors. Two months later, Character announced [c.ai+](https://blog.character.ai/introducing-c-ai/?ref=bondoro.com), an opt-in subscription plan, and released its first iOS and Android apps. The Debtor reports approximately 12 million monthly active users worldwide, who spend approximately 120 minutes a day on the platform on average. Revenue comes primarily from subscriptions and in-app advertising, with in-app purchases added in early 2026, and totaled approximately $23.6 million in fiscal year 2025. > [Character Technologies, Inc.](https://app.bondoro.com/preview/cases/Character_Technologies_Inc?ref=bondoro.com) filed for Chapter 11 protection on October 12, 2026 (the "Petition Date") in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, reporting $50 million to $100 million in both assets and liabilities. --- ### **Corporate History** ##### The 2024 Google Transaction In August 2024, Character entered into a transaction with Google (the “2024 Transaction”) in which Google paid approximately [$2.7 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204424000118/goog-20240930.htm?ref=bondoro.com) in cash for a non-exclusive license to Character’s large language model (“LLM”) technology and a release of certain claims Character may have had against Google and certain other parties, and rehired Character’s founders. The 2024 Transaction also served as a liquidity event for Character’s shareholders. Its venture investors were reportedly bought out at a valuation of approximately [$2.5 billion](https://www.axios.com/2024/08/05/google-characterai-venture-capital?ref=bondoro.com), and [EM360Tech](https://em360tech.com/tech-articles/character-ai-scraps-building-llms-after-google-deal?ref=bondoro.com), reporting on interim CEO Dominic Perella's interview with the Financial Times, said Character used the proceeds to fund that buyout, transfer ownership to employees through a co-operative structure and make a one-off payout to staff, while approximately 20% of its employees left for Google DeepMind. Consistent with those reports, all of Character’s equity holders as of the Petition Date are current or former directors or employees, and no corporation owns 10% or more of the Debtor. The 2024 Transaction also marked the end of Character’s effort to build its own models. Before the deal, Character trained its own LLM from scratch, according to [Andreessen Horowitz](https://a16z.com/2023/03/23/investing-in-character-ai/?ref=b...

LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # New AI Shield MIRAGE Fights Hidden Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![New AI Shield MIRAGE Fights Hidden Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-6070-750x422.png) New AI Shield MIRAGE Fights Hidden Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, has become the workhorse technology that lets large language models reach beyond their training data. By retrieving documents from an external knowledge base, filtering and reranking them, assembling them into context, and then generating an answer with post-hoc verification, RAG systems power mainstream AI products such as ChatGPT and Perplexity.ai as well as countless enterprise knowledge bases. Yet the very openness that makes RAG useful also makes it dangerous. A new study published in the journal Cybersecurity introduces MIRAGE, a two-stage adaptive defense framework designed to counter a class of attacks that conventional filters barely notice: textual evidence manipulation. The threat was systematized by the SafeRAG benchmark, which identified four novel attack types that abandon overt malicious signals in favor of stealth. Silver noise embeds partially correct, highly relevant information so that malicious fragments rank well in relevance scoring and slip past filters while diluting valid evidence. Inter-context conflict plants subtle contradictions across multiple retrieved passages, exploiting weaknesses in how language models reconcile conflicting sources. Soft advertisement weaves implicit promotional or toxic language into otherwise compliant text, evading standard toxicity detectors. White Denial-of-Service, or White DoS, disguises fabricated safety warnings as compliance alerts, tricking the model into refusing to answer altogether and degrading the availability of the entire system. Each of these attacks targets the blind spots of defenses built to catch obviously irrelevant or overtly violating content, rendering components such as natural language inference filters and knowledge compressors largely ineffective. Existing multi-stage defense frameworks, including TrustRAG, which cleans retrieved evidence through clustering, integrates knowledge, and performs consistency self-verification, were never designed with these covert patterns in mind. Their clustering and filtering mechanisms rely on fixed parameters that cannot simultaneously handle multi-document clustered contamination, typical of silver noise and inter-context conflict, and single-document embedded manipulation, typical of soft advertisement and White DoS. Their generic integration rules provide no targeted handling for implicit contradictions, subtle manipulative phrasing, or induced refusals. And their post-hoc verification typically checks only factual consistency, overlooking implicit toxicity and availability risks. The result is a defense that either misses malicious chunks or discards valid evidence, and that can still be steered by a false evidence chain or quietly degraded by refusal induction. MIRAGE, developed by researchers at Information Engineering University in Zhengzhou and the Institute of Information Engineering of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, attacks the problem in two chained stages. The first stage, clean retrieval, begins by embedding the retrieved documents and computing the local density of each document in the embedding space. Because different attacks leave different distributional fingerprints, this density analysis allows the framework to predict the attack type before filtering begins. AI Product.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Panopto launches AI tools to unlock video libraries](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/08/stephen-laster-story-320930.webp) [ERP](https://itbrief.asia/tag/enterprise-resource-planning) [GenAI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/generative-ai) [AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/artificial-intelligence) # Panopto launches AI tools to unlock video libraries Thu, 15th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Sofiah Nichole Salivio](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--3f3cbcdb3f86206827b894ccc07566b24a1d49e6/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/unnamed%20(2).webp) SOFIAH NICHOLE SALIVIO News Editor](/author/sofiah-nichole-salivio) Panopto has launched three new video knowledge tools: Folio, AI Search and MCP Server. The products are designed to help organisations and educational institutions use recorded video content more easily. The releases are meant to address a common problem in teaching and workplace training: large libraries of recorded lectures, training sessions and other internal videos often contain useful information, but users can struggle to find specific answers quickly. Folio turns existing video material into study aids such as study guides, flashcards and practice quizzes. It also includes an AI tutor grounded in the source material, allowing users to work from content already stored in a Panopto library rather than relying on a general-purpose AI service. Organizations now rely on AI across nearly every function, including sales, marketing, finance, customer service, and operations. But as adoption has accelerated, a different challenge has emerged. The question is no longer whether organizations have AI in their tech stack. It’s whether the growing collection of AI systems, business applications and enterprise data can work together effectively and securely. The next phase of enterprise AI won’t be defined by who builds the smartest assistant or the latest and greatest feature. It will be defined by how effectively organizations integrate intelligence across the enterprise. ## **The Fast Times of AI Integration** Enterprise software vendors have spent the past few years racing to launch new AI features and to embed AI assistants, chat interfaces, and automation into their platforms. No one wanted to risk falling behind. But while AI’s use cases are delivering meaningful productivity gains, they’re still largely confined to individual applications because these solutions were often stood up quickly, tacked onto existing platforms, and built in silos. The result is a growing number of AI solutions across enterprise software that often weren’t designed for interoperability. This means that as teams adopted AI, a new reality emerged: employees work across multiple systems, and no department relies on a single solution. Take sales, for instance. One sales opportunity touches marketing, sales, finance, customer success, legal, and operations. Compounding this issue is that most organizations didn’t just adopt one or two solutions; they’ve adopted dozens and now must figure out how to make their new ecosystem function as a single connected system. ## **Enterprise AI Runs on Context, Not Applications** The challenge here isn’t just that organizations now have too many AI tools. It’s that AI is only as effective as the information it can access. That’s why interoperability is critical. Unlike traditional software solutions, AI doesn’t operate in isolation. It needs to see the bigger picture, including how marketing campaigns are impacting revenue, how new investments are streamlining operations, and how new product launches are resonating with customers. That context is often spread across dozens of applications, each with its own data model, permissions, and governance policies. AI Product.content: ![](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/security_g1192070289_searchsitetablet_520X173.jpg) Getty Images/iStockphoto # Bug bounty reckoning: AI slop forces enterprise strategy shift ## As AI fills bug bounty queues with low-quality report slop, tech giants like Intel and Google are rethinking paid rewards and shifting toward automated internal defenses. ![Dan Raywood](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/computerweekly/dan-raywood-cw-contributor.jpg) As generative AI tools flood vulnerability intake pipelines with plausible-looking "slop," tech giants are reconsidering the ROI of traditional, paid bug bounty programs. Between external triage exhaustion and the rise of internal automated AI auditing, industry heavyweights like Intel and Google are forcing a rewrite of vulnerability disclosure rules. What began as isolated adjustments could herald an industry-wide pivot. Earlier this year, Curl creator Daniel Stenberg shut down the project's bug bounty program after being overwhelmed by a flood of LLM-generated false positives. By mid-September, reports surfaced that Intel had quietly suspended cash rewards for its long-running bug bounty program. Weeks later, on October 1, Google [stopped accepting vulnerability reports](https://x.com/GoogleVRP/status/2105689195180179605) for its own Open-Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP), explicitly citing an unsustainable influx of invalid, automated reports. Together, these moves mark a turning point in vulnerability management. Security teams are facing an asymmetric resource drain in which low-effort AI reports cost submitters almost nothing to generate but require hundreds of expensive engineering hours to manually review and debunk. ## Triage under pressure Intel's sudden pause on paid bug bounties is one of the most prominent casualties of this shifting operational landscape. In a statement to *TechTarget*, the tech giant said: "As part of an ongoing review of how the [bug bounty](https://www.computerweekly.com/opinion/Why-bug-bounty-programmes-are-essential-for-cyber-resilience) program can best support Intel's broader product security efforts, Intel has paused the program until further notice. Intel will continue to honor existing bug bounty commitments and accept security reports through its Vulnerability Disclosure Program." Intel did not respond to a follow-up question about whether the decision had been prompted by an increase in the use of AI tools to discover vulnerabilities. However, Kara Sprague, CEO of HackerOne -- the platform hosting Intel's rewards program -- confirmed that submission volumes across enterprise programs are surging. "More of them look credible at first glance but were never tested against the target or are outside the program's scope: a report can now be written in minutes," she said. "Validating it still takes what it always did: reproducing the finding, confirming the impact and deciding whether it needs a fix. That is the constraint on every program right now, and it is the work we have built our platform around." Industry data underscores the sheer scale of this vulnerability disclosure bottleneck. According to a recent [report from Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/vulnerability-discovery-and-exploitation-trends-in-the-ai-era), the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month doubled between January and July 2026, rising from 5,045 in January to 10,477 in July, before climbing further to 10,740 in August. ## The shift to internal auditing As the maintainers of Curl discovered, a substantial increase in submissions takes critical time away from the analysts and researchers who must review each report. As a result, the emphasis is shifting towards ensuring that submissions meet specific criteria and reducing the time spent assessing reports that do not identify genuine vulnerabilities. A jailbroken PlayStation 5 is now running a 27 billion parameter AI model Developer cobanov's open source PS5LM project runs Qwen3.8-27B at over 20 tokens per second on a jailbroken console's GPU, up from roughly one token a minute when the same model ran on the CPU alone. ![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/elroy.png) [Elroy Fernandes](https://startupfortune.com/author/elroy/) · 5 min read · 589 reads ![A jailbroken PlayStation 5 is now running a 27 billion parameter AI model](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ps5lm-qwen3-8-27b-jailbroken-ps5-ai-model-1024x576.jpg) *An open source fork of PS5LM has turned Sony's locked-down console into a working local AI server, no cloud bill, no gaming PC required.* Plug a PS5 into the same Wi-Fi network as your laptop, open a browser, and you can now chat with a 27-billion-parameter language model running entirely on hardware most people bought to play Spider-Man. The GPU version is a fork called PS5LM Plus, maintained on GitHub by abhi245y and built on PS5LM, Mert Cobanov's llama.cpp port for jailbroken PS5s. The headline number: Qwen3.8-27B, a large open-weight model from Alibaba's Qwen team, generates text at roughly 20 tokens per second when it runs on the console's GPU. That is not a typo. And it is not a simulation running on some hidden PC. The PS5 ships with an AMD GPU carrying 16GB of GDDR6 memory and 448 GB/s of bandwidth, which is exactly the kind of spec sheet that matters for running a large language model. Token generation is bound by memory bandwidth more than raw compute, and Sony's console happens to have plenty of it sitting idle most of the time a game isn't loaded. Getting there required stacking several independent pieces of PS5 hacking work on top of each other. The setup starts with a jailbroken console, and the Relapse browser exploit now covers firmware versions 7.00 through 13.60. The original PS5LM payload is built with the open source ps5-payload-dev SDK, while the GPU fork runs as a native homebrew app. The PS5's operating system is based on FreeBSD and runs on an 8-core AMD Zen 2 CPU. Standard llama.cpp code compiles for it with only minor changes. That's the quieter half of the story: a game console running a modified BSD kernel under the hood turns out to be a far friendlier target for porting Linux-world software than most people...

It gives type-safe, provider-agnostic tools for calling models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others with a simple decorator or model object. You define prompts as functions, add tools with @llm.tool, request structured output via Pydantic, stream responses, and build agent loops by repeatedly calling execute\_tools and resume. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) # Inditex Open-Sources Code, Backs €1.7B Platform [2026] * [![Elias Virtanen](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/plugins/one-user-avatar/assets/images/wpua-64x64.png)](https://tech-insider.org/author/elias-virtanen/)[Elias Virtanen](https://tech-insider.org/author/elias-virtanen/ "Posts by Elias Virtanen") * [Software](https://tech-insider.org/category/software/) [Elias Virtanen](https://tech-insider.org/author/elias-virtanen/) October 14, 2026 14 min read Inditex, the Spanish retail group behind Zara, Massimo Dutti and Pull&Bear, is pushing further into open source software as part of a broader technology strategy shift, according to reports from The World’s Fashion Business News and Chatham House on October 14, 2026. The move formalizes something Inditex has been building quietly for years: a dedicated internal body that decides which code the company writes for itself is also useful to the wider software community, and then publishes it for anyone to inspect, use or contribute to. For a company best known for fast fashion logistics rather than developer tooling, the news is a notable signal. Inditex open source software is no longer a side project run by a handful of engineers with GitHub access. It is coordinated centrally, documented publicly, and tied to a multi-billion-euro digital infrastructure bet the company made years before most retailers took “platform engineering” seriously. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. [Add Now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Ftech-insider.org%2F) ## What Inditex Actually Announced At the center of the story is a simple idea: Inditex publishes software it considers useful beyond its own teams so others can use, inspect and contribute to it. That is not a slogan invented for a press release, it is the operating principle the company has attached to its public code repositories. The practical result is a growing catalog of projects, tools, and reference libraries that any developer, not just Inditex employees, can pull down, read, and build on. The timing matters. Retailers of Inditex’s size have historically treated their internal engineering as a competitive black box, worth protecting rather than publishing. The shift toward Inditex open source software suggests the company now sees developer goodwill, external contributions, and recruiting leverage as worth more than the marginal secrecy of code that is not, by itself, a fashion business advantage. ## Inside Inditex’s Open Source Office (OSO) The governance piece of the story is the Open Source Office, known internally as the OSO. Inditex’s open-source activity is coordinated by this office, which functions as the clearinghouse for what gets published, under what license, and with what level of ongoing maintenance commitment. Large companies that open source code without this kind of structure tend to end up with abandoned repositories and inconsistent licensing, which damages trust with the very developer community they are trying to court. By centralizing that decision-making, Inditex is following a pattern more associated with large technology firms than apparel retailers. The OSO’s existence is the clearest evidence that Inditex open source software is now a standing program rather than an improvised list of repositories some engineering team happened to make public. ## The FOSS Manifesto: Inditex’s Public Rulebook for Giving Away Code Inditex maintains a repository containing its FOSS Manifesto, along with documentation and templates for open-sourc...

Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Tech firms launch custom AI chips for data centre inference Microsoft announced its Maia 300 custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip, designed for AI models across its data centres. The company plans large-scale deployments of its Azure Maia systems in 2027. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 14, 2026 at 09:00 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Microsoft announced Maia 300, its next-generation custom AI chip for data centre workloads. * Large-scale deployments of Azure Maia systems are planned for 2027, becoming the primary inference platform. * Google, Amazon, and OpenAI are also deploying custom chips to control AI inference costs and efficiency. * The shift aims to improve computing per dollar spent and manage power consumption in data centres. [Microsoft](/tag/microsoft) has announced Maia 300, its next-generation custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip, designed to run AI models across its data centres. The company plans to begin large-scale deployments of its Azure Maia systems in 2027. These chips are expected to become the primary inference platform for its products and services. Other major technology companies are also deploying custom chips for [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference). These include [Google](/tag/google) with its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and [Amazon](/tag/amazon) with its Trainium chips. [OpenAI](/tag/openai) also plans an inference chip, Jalapeño, with Broadcom. This shift is driven by the need to control inference costs, improve efficiency, and gain greater control over hardware supply and infrastructure planning. AI computing involves training models and then using them for inference tasks. Inference becomes a recurring operating expense as AI tools become more widely used. Every query or AI interaction consumes computing resources. Custom chips can be designed around a company's models, software, and expected workloads. This potentially improves computing delivered per rupee or dollar spent on hardware and electricity. Power consumption is another key consideration for data centres. Improving AI tokens generated per unit of energy can help companies serve more requests within existing power constraints. Custom silicon provides greater control over hardware supply and infrastructure planning. Companies may reduce external accelerator purchases and optimise system interaction. However, chip design involves significant development costs and manufacturing considerations. These factors affect the final budget. Microsoft's Maia 300 builds on earlier Maia processors. Maia 200 is already serving production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot. The Maia 300 architecture is designed for long-context reasoning and memory-intensive processing. Its planned uses include Copilot and GitHub Copilot. Microsoft's strategy coordinates chip design with its cloud infrastructure and AI software. This allows it to optimise the entire system for its services. Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Innovation, told Axios that Microsoft prioritises Maia for inference. She described it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing. Google has developed TPUs for years and uses them to support its AI models. In April 2026, Google announced its eighth-generation TPU systems, TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference. Amazon is pursuing a similar strategy with its Trainium family. He urged Korea to advance domestic AI semiconductors so they can be used for model training as well as inference, and to secure infrastructure software capabilities to connect and operate multiple chips efficiently. He backed government efforts on foundation models and domestic AI chips, and proposed boosting domestic token demand, including through token vouchers. * Writer Son Seul-gi * published 2026-10-15 07:30:00 Share this article ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202610/707124_654827_2730.jpg) Jo Kang-won (조강원), CEO of Moreh. [Photo: Moreh] "It is hard to complete sovereign AI in the true sense with only proprietary AI model development. It is also worth noting that Korea should advance technology so domestically made AI semiconductors can be used not only for inference but also for model training. Korea also needs to secure infrastructure software capabilities to efficiently connect and operate multiple semiconductors to build a Korean-style 'full-stack sovereign AI.'" Jo Kang-won (조강원), CEO of Moreh, recently met with a reporter and said Korea is the country closest to having the capabilities to realise sovereign AI, excluding the United States and China. He stressed that Korea needs proprietary technologies not only in semiconductors and models but also in data centres and software. Moreh is an infrastructure software company that supports the efficient use of AI semiconductors from different manufacturers in a single data centre. It is developing technology to run AI models not only on Nvidia graphics processing units but also on chips from AMD and Tenstorrent. It also optimises computing tasks to lower data centre operating costs. Jo gave a positive assessment of government policies to develop proprietary AI foundation models and foster domestic AI semiconductors. He said few countries other than the United States and China have so many companies competing in both areas, and that Korea is building a foundation to realise full-stack sovereign AI. He stressed that developing proprietary AI models is also essential. He said Korea should not assume foreign companies will continue to disclose the latest models indefinitely. He said, "If we can steadily keep up with the global leading models with a gap of 3 months or 6 months, it will greatly help maintain the competitiveness of domestic companies." He said domestic companies, including Samsung Electronics, should be able to use AI models close to the global leading group while processing sensitive industrial data in their own data centres without sending it outside. Jo stressed that technological self-reliance should expand beyond AI models to the entire supply chain. He said Korea should build on capabilities it has already accumulated in semiconductors and infrastructure software and also take on the challenge of full-stack sovereign AI. To do that, lowering dependence on foreign semiconductors from the model-training stage is a task. Nvidia and other foreign GPUs are mainly used for AI model training in Korea. Domestic neural processing unit design companies such as Rebellion and FuriosaAI are also focusing their businesses on the inference market rather than large-scale pre-training. (Microsoft)](/news/photo/202610/278842_286549_541.jpg) Microsoft’s Azure Maia 300 AI chip, designed to improve inference performance and reduce reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs. (Microsoft) Microsoft is mounting a direct challenge to Nvidia’s market dominance with the unveiling of its next-generation proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) chip, the Maia 300. As one of Nvidia’s largest customers, Microsoft plans to significantly increase its use of in-house chips, a move expected to reshape supply chain dynamics across the AI semiconductor market. On Oct. 12 (local time), Microsoft unveiled the Maia 300, its third-generation AI accelerator, and announced plans to use it as the primary AI inference system across its products and services. With full-scale production and deployment set to begin in 2027, more than 1 million units of the Maia 300 are expected to be supplied that year alone. Scott Guthrie, executive vice president of Microsoft’s Cloud and AI division, said, “We are entering a new phase of infrastructure as the era of superintelligence approaches,” emphasizing that the Maia 300 would process 40% more tokens per megawatt (MW) than leading graphics processing unit (GPU)-based systems. The Maia 300 incorporates cutting-edge technical specifications. Its computing chiplets, which handle core processing tasks, use TSMC’s 2-nanometer-class (N2P) process, while chiplets responsible for functions such as data movement use a 3-nanometer process, forming a multi-chiplet architecture. A key feature is the integration of eight HBM4 stacks, the sixth generation of high-bandwidth memory, delivering memory bandwidth of 18 terabytes (TB) per second. Power efficiency and processing capacity have also been substantially improved. A single rack housing 96 accelerators consumes approximately 167 kilowatts (kW) of power while delivering up to seven times the token throughput of its predecessor, the Maia 200. Microsoft designed the chip around an inference-first architecture optimized for AI workloads requiring long-context processing and memory-intensive computation, focusing on reducing service operating costs. Microsoft is not alone in developing proprietary AI chips. Google already operates Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) optimized for both training and inference workloads, while Amazon supports major partners such as Anthropic through its proprietary Trainium chips. OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, is collaborating with Broadcom to develop its own inference-specialized chip, Jalapeño, while Meta and Anthropic have also begun internally exploring chip design initiatives. These companies are focusing particularly on inference because the proliferation of AI agents is driving a sharp increase in the computing power required to generate responses. Their reasoning is that processing more responses using the same amount of power can improve the profitability of AI service operations. Rani Borkar, president of Microsoft Azure Hardware Systems, said that securing a competitive advantage requires designing the entire system together, encompassing not only chips but also memory, networking and power consumption. Logo, Korea JoongAng Daily](/view-resources/dachser2/public/koreajoongangdaily/logo.svg)](https://www.koreajoongangdaily.com) # SK hynix sees 20-fold AI infrastructure growth The chipmaker forecasts a 20-fold increase in AI infrastructure performance by 2030 as inference demand drives new memory needs. Published [Make us preferred on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=koreajoongangdaily.com) ![SK hynix headquarters in Icheon, Gyeonggi, on Aug. 24](https://image.koreajoongangdaily.com/12904676.webp?imageId=12904676&width=960&height=548&format=jpg) SK hynix headquarters in Icheon, Gyeonggi, on Aug. 24 NEWS1 SK hynix projected Wednesday that the performance scale of AI infrastructure will grow roughly 20-fold by 2030, driven by rapidly rising demand for AI inference. Ahn Hyun, head of development at the Korean chip giant, made the projection during his keynote speech at the 2026 Semiconductor Exhibition, which opened earlier in the day for a three-day run in southern Seoul. Ahn said the AI inference market is expanding simultaneously in three areas — task complexity, the amount of information processed at a time and the volume of inference requests. ## Related Article * [### Humanoid robots eyed as next driver of memory chip demand](/business/humanoid-robots-eyed-as-next-driver-of-memory-chip-demand/12915302) * [### SK chief vows to accelerate Honam chip cluster construction as semiconductor demand surges worldwide](/business/sk-chief-vows-to-accelerate-honam-chip-cluster-construction-as-semiconductor-demand-surges-worldwide/12912920) * [### SK hynix shareholders move to block Solidigm Nasdaq listing over dilution fears](/business/sk-hynix-shareholders-move-to-block-solidigm-nasdaq-listing-over-dilution-fears/12904620) The interaction of the three factors is rapidly increasing demand for AI infrastructure, he said. As demand for AI inference surges, memory is becoming increasingly important for storing and transferring large volumes of data. In particular, the growing capacity requirements of key-value caches, which store and reuse information previously processed by AI models, are requiring data to be distributed across different types of memory, including high bandwidth memory (HBM), dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) and solid-state drives. SK hynix is pursuing next-generation memory technologies, including 3-D stacked DRAM and high bandwidth flash, while continuing to enhance the performance of existing HBM products, the executive added.
